newsitem.title: SOMALIA: Australian freed after four months in Somali jail.
newsitem.headline: Australian freed after four months in Somali jail.

text.p: An Australian pilot held in jail in Somalia for more than four months was freed on Thursday, flown to Kenya and handed over by Kenya's president to his ambassador.
Australian High Commissioner John Trotter told Reuters Justin Fraser, 25, was flown to Nairobi after Kenyan President Daniel arap Moi requested his release by faction leader Hussein Aideed.

"I was called to State House (in Nairobi) and went to see the president who handed Fraser over to me so I just handed him over to his family," said Trotter. He said Fraser was thin but mentally alert although he appeared tired and needed sleep.
"I am delighted and thankful to President Moi," said Trotter, adding Fraser said he was woken up at 3 a.m. (0000 GMT) on Thursday and flown to Nairobi, apparently from the capital, Mogadishu.
"The president said he had spoken to Hussein Aideed and suggested that he let him go and he had agreed," Trotter added.
Fraser was handed over to his Australian mother who has been staying in Nairobi for months and campaigning for his release, which came as a complete surprise after numerous false alarms.
He had been held since May in the southwestern Somali town of Baidoa by the south Mogadishu-based faction led by Aideed, who succeeded his father Mohamed Farah Aideed at his death on August 1.
Hussein Aideed said in late August that the Australian might be released within a few weeks after a review of his case and appeals from visiting U.N. officials and Somalis living abroad.

Fraser, 25, was forced by mechanical problems to land at an airstrip in May in the western town of Huddur and was sentenced to 25 years in jail and a fine of $485,000 in Baidoa for violating Somali airspace.
Fraser's plane was loaded with qat, the leaves and bark of a bush which when chewed acts as a mild stimulant. It is flown to Somalia daily in a multi-million dollar business from Kenya and Ethiopia.
Moi's office said Fraser was handed over to Trotter after 129 days in captivity in an emotional ceremony after Australia had failed to secure his release through other intermediaries.

"The Kenyan head of state negotiated with the current leaders of the United Somali Congress and Somali National Alliance, that is Hussein Aideed, who granted the president's request," it added in a statement.
It said that Fraser was brought to Nairobi by a personal representative of Aideed's and the release was a sign of the high esteem that the Somali leader had for the Kenyan president.
It quoted Fraser as saying at State House words alone could not express adequately his debt of gratitude to Moi and as a non-Kenyan he felt overwhelmed the president had done such a thing.

It was the first time that Moi's direct intervention had secured the release of a foreigner held in Somalia and was apparently related to the desire of Hussein Aideed, a 34-year-old former U.S. marine, to improve external relations.
Australia said in June Fraser was very sick and held in a militia jail in Baidoa, which Mohamed Farah Aideed's forces seized in September last year after thrusting out of Mogadishu.
The Aideed government is only recognised by Sudan and Libya.

Mohamed Farah Aideed's government jailed several foreigners accused of entering Somalia illegally. All were freed after negotiations. Kidnappings especially involving foreigners are very common in Somalia, where weapons are readily available.
